newsitem.title: NIGER: Niger chooses new parliament, opposition boycotts.
newsitem.headline: Niger chooses new parliament, opposition boycotts.

text.p: Voters in the West African nation of Niger cast their ballots for a new national assembly on Saturday with coupmaker-turned-president Ibrahim Bare Mainassara urging a huge turnout despite an opposition boycott.

"I hope that the people of Niger will turn out massively to vote so we can extricate ourselves from this never-ending cycle of elections and devote ourselves to reviving the economy," the president said after casting his vote in the capital Niamey's town hall.
Saturday's poll was the third parliamentary election in this vast, poverty-stricken and mainly Moslem nation in three years.
As in previous elections, initial turnout in Niamey was low but polling stations opened on time, witnesses said.
Despite a chaotic July presidential election, which politicians accused Mainassara of rigging, security force presence in the capital was light and confined to polling stations.

Opposition politicians, including Mahamane Ousmane the elected civilian president Mainassara ousted in January, refused to register for Saturday's poll demanding that the result of the July presidential election be scrapped.
"I regret this because I had hoped that all Niger citizens would rally round a consensus to organise this poll," Mainassara said, adding that he believed the opposition had never intended to stand.

Negotiations between the two sides collapsed after repeated extensions of the registration date with the opposition Front for the Restoration and Defence of Democracy standing by its demands, which also included reinstatement of a scrapped independent electoral commission.

In July, Mainassara suspended the electoral commission on the second day of polling, accusing it of irregularities, and placed his opponents under house arrest. He appointed a new commission which declared him winner with 52.22 percent of votes cast.
The United States said the election was fraudulent and suspended development aid. It has warned its nationals here to take precautions on Saturday.
"The possibility exists that campaign activities and demonstrations could turn unruly and result in some form of civil unrest," the U.S. Embassy in Niamey said.
A total of 220 candidates from around a dozen parties are running for the 83-seat assembly, including the Union of Independents for Democratic Renewal which supports Mainassara.
Around 3.8 million people are eligible to vote at more than 8,300 polling stations. Niger closed its borders for the poll.
Like many of its neighbours in sub-Saharan Africa, Niger launched democratic reforms in the 1990s after the collapse of Communist rule in the Soviet Union.

It held presidential and parliamentary elections in 1993 but government became paralysed by squabbling between Mahamane and his prime minister Amadou Hama who was from a rival group which gained a majority in parliament.
Early parliamentary elections in January 1995 failed to resolve the standoff and Mainassara seized power a year later, drawing widespread international criticism.
Polls opened on Saturday at 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) and close at 7 p.m. (1800 GMT). Provisional results, which have to be verified by the Supreme Court, could be known within 48 hours.
